sla_notes_intro: Economics is the study of how people, firms and governments use scarce resources to satisfy unlimited wants. This activity introduces its meaning, origin, scope and basic terms.
sla_notes_details: Economics is the social science that studies how society allocates scarce resources among competing uses to satisfy human wants. It began as political economy; Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations (1776) is regarded as the start of modern economics, and the word comes from the Greek oikonomia, management of a household. Basic terms include want, need, scarcity, choice, opportunity cost (the value of the next best alternative given up), goods, services, utility, production, consumption and exchange. The central economic problem is scarcity, giving rise to the fundamental questions: what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce. The branches are microeconomics (individual consumers, firms and markets) and macroeconomics (the whole economy: income, employment, prices, growth, trade), with positive economics dealing with facts and normative economics with value judgments. Economics is related to mathematics, statistics, geography, history, political science and sociology. Its importance is to help individuals, firms and governments make rational decisions, plan and evaluate development policies.
sla_notes_illustrations: A farmer with one hectare and money for either maize seeds or tomato seeds must choose. If he plants maize the opportunity cost is the profit that tomatoes would have earned; this shows scarcity, choice and opportunity cost together.
sla_notes_daily_life: Every household uses economics when deciding how to spend a limited monthly income, and governments use it when allocating a budget among education, health and roads.
sla_exercise: Define economics.::The study of how society uses scarce resources to satisfy unlimited human wants.||What is opportunity cost?::The value of the next best alternative that is given up when a choice is made.||Name the three fundamental economic questions.::What to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce.||Differentiate microeconomics from macroeconomics.::Microeconomics studies individual units such as consumers, firms and markets, while macroeconomics studies the whole economy such as national income, unemployment and inflation.

sla_notes_intro: An economic system is the way a society organises the production, distribution and consumption of goods and services. Different systems answer the basic economic questions in different ways.
sla_notes_details: The main forms are traditional, capitalist (free market), socialist (command or planned) and mixed economies. In a traditional system decisions follow custom and production is by subsistence farming, hunting or herding. In capitalism resources are privately owned, the price mechanism directs production, and the motive is profit; its advantages are efficiency, consumer choice and innovation, while its disadvantages are inequality, unemployment and monopoly power. In socialism the state owns the main means of production and plans output; its advantages are equity and full employment, while its disadvantages are lack of incentives, shortages and low efficiency. A mixed economy combines private enterprise with government participation, providing public goods and regulating markets; it is the most common form today, and Tanzania moved from a socialist policy under the Arusha Declaration (1967) to a market-oriented mixed economy after the 1980s reforms.
sla_notes_illustrations: In a market economy the price of bread rises when demand rises, signalling producers to bake more, whereas in a command economy a planning committee would set the quantity and price of bread.
sla_notes_daily_life: The system determines what goods appear in shops, who owns land and industries and how the government taxes and spends, which affects people's jobs and prices.
sla_exercise: Name the four main economic systems.::Traditional, capitalist (market), socialist (command) and mixed economies.||Give two advantages of a free market economy.::Efficiency in resource allocation and wide consumer choice (also innovation).||State two disadvantages of a command economy.::Lack of incentives and shortages or inefficiency in production.||Why is a mixed economy common today?::It combines the efficiency of private markets with government provision of public goods and regulation.

sla_notes_intro: Microeconomics studies the decisions of individual economic units: consumers, households and firms, and how they interact in markets. It explains prices and the allocation of resources at the small scale.
sla_notes_details: The meaning of microeconomics is the study of individual decision-making units and the markets in which they trade. Its scope includes the theory of consumer behaviour, demand and supply, price determination, theory of production and costs, market structures, factor pricing (wages, rent, interest and profit) and welfare economics. Its goals include efficient allocation of resources, consumer satisfaction (utility maximisation), profit maximisation by firms, fair distribution of income and consumer protection. Assumptions such as ceteris paribus (other things being equal) and rational behaviour are used to build simple models. Methods include graphs, tables and equations, and microeconomic principles are used by managers and government agencies for pricing, taxation and regulation.
sla_notes_illustrations: A household with a monthly budget of 200 000 shillings chooses between rice, beans and transport; it allocates money so that the last shilling spent on each gives equal satisfaction, applying the tenets of consumer choice.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding microeconomics helps a person compare prices, run a small business, choose an occupation and understand why fuel or food prices change.
sla_exercise: Define microeconomics.::The study of individual economic units such as consumers, firms and markets.||Give two topics covered in microeconomics.::Demand and supply, theory of production and costs, market structures or factor pricing.||State two goals of microeconomics.::Efficient resource allocation and maximising consumer satisfaction and firms' profits.||What does ceteris paribus mean?::Other things remaining constant.

sla_notes_intro: Price theory explains how prices are determined by the interaction of demand and supply and how sensitive quantities are to price changes.
sla_notes_details: Demand is the quantity of a good consumers are willing and able to buy at each price, and the law of demand says that quantity demanded falls when price rises, ceteris paribus. Supply is the quantity producers are willing to offer at each price, and the law of supply says that quantity supplied rises when price rises. Market equilibrium is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied; a price above it creates a surplus and a price below it creates a shortage. Non-price factors shift curves: income, tastes, prices of related goods and population shift demand; costs, technology, taxes and weather shift supply. Price elasticity of demand (PED) = percentage change in quantity demanded / percentage change in price; demand is elastic if PED is greater than 1, inelastic if less than 1 and unitary if equal to 1. Other elasticities are income, cross and price elasticity of supply.
sla_notes_illustrations: If Qd = 100 - 2P and Qs = 20 + 2P then equilibrium is when 100 - 2P = 20 + 2P, so 4P = 80, P = 20 and Q = 60. If the price of a good rises from 10 to 12 and the quantity demanded falls from 100 to 80, PED = 20%/20% = 1, unitary elasticity.
sla_notes_daily_life: Price theory explains why the price of tomatoes falls in the harvest season, why fuel price increases reduce car use and how a shopkeeper decides whether to raise prices.
sla_exercise: State the law of demand.::When the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls, ceteris paribus.||Find equilibrium price and quantity if Qd = 100 - 2P and Qs = 20 + 2P.::P = 20 and Q = 60.||Find PED if price rises from 10 to 12 and quantity demanded falls from 100 to 80.::Percentage change in quantity = 20% and in price = 20%, so PED = 1.||Give two factors which shift the demand curve.::Changes in consumer income and changes in tastes (also prices of related goods or population).

sla_notes_intro: Production theory studies how firms combine factors of production to produce output, and cost theory studies the expenses of production and the revenue and profit that result.
sla_notes_details: The factors of production are land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship, earning rent, wages, interest and profit. The production function shows the relationship between inputs and output, Q = f(land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship). In the short run at least one factor is fixed and the law of diminishing returns states that adding more of a variable factor to a fixed factor eventually reduces the marginal product. Average product AP = Q/L and marginal product MP = change in Q / change in L. Firms aim at profit maximisation, but some pursue sales, growth or social objectives. In the long run all factors are variable and returns to scale may be increasing, constant or decreasing, with economies and diseconomies of scale. Costs: total cost TC = fixed cost FC + variable cost VC; average cost AC = TC/Q; marginal cost MC = change in TC / change in Q. Revenue: TR = P x Q, AR = TR/Q, MR = change in TR / change in Q; profit = TR - TC and is maximised where MR = MC.
sla_notes_illustrations: If labour of 1, 2 and 3 workers gives output of 10, 22 and 30 units, the marginal products are 10, 12 and 8, showing diminishing returns after the second worker. A firm with FC = 1 000 and VC = 2 000 at 50 units has TC = 3 000 and AC = 60.
sla_notes_daily_life: A bakery that adds more workers in one small oven finds each extra worker adds less output, so the owner compares extra cost with extra revenue when deciding how many workers to hire.
sla_exercise: State the law of diminishing returns.::When more units of a variable factor are added to a fixed factor, the marginal product eventually falls.||A firm has FC = 1 000 and VC = 2 000 at 50 units. Find AC.::TC = 3 000 so AC = 3 000/50 = 60.||At what output is profit maximised?::Where marginal revenue equals marginal cost (MR = MC).||Name the four factors of production and their rewards.::Land (rent), labour (wages), capital (interest) and entrepreneurship (profit).

sla_notes_intro: A market is any arrangement that brings buyers and sellers together to exchange goods and services. Markets differ by what is traded and by how competitive they are.
sla_notes_details: A market does not need a fixed place; it can be physical (a village market) or virtual (online shopping or mobile money trading). Types by commodity include goods, services, labour, money and capital markets, and by area they can be local, national or international. Market structures describe the degree of competition. Perfect competition has many buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, free entry and exit and perfect knowledge, so firms are price takers. Monopoly has one seller with barriers to entry and price-making power. Monopolistic competition has many firms selling differentiated products, like restaurants or clothing shops. Oligopoly has a few large firms that depend on one another, such as mobile network companies or breweries, and it may involve collusion or price wars. Efficiency, consumer welfare and price differ among the structures; perfect competition gives the lowest price while monopoly may charge a higher price and restrict output.
sla_notes_illustrations: A maize market with hundreds of small farmers selling identical grain is close to perfect competition, while a single electricity supplier in a region illustrates monopoly.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding market structure helps consumers know why mobile data prices are similar across networks and why governments regulate monopolies such as utilities.
sla_exercise: Define a market.::Any arrangement that brings buyers and sellers together for exchange.||Give three features of perfect competition.::Many buyers and sellers, homogeneous product, and free entry and exit.||Which market structure has a few large interdependent firms?::Oligopoly.||Name one example of a monopoly.::A single electricity or water supplier in an area.

sla_notes_intro: Each economic system allocates resources and distributes income in a different way. This activity examines how markets, planning and mixed arrangements decide who gets what.
sla_notes_details: In a market economy the price mechanism allocates resources: high prices attract resources to profitable uses and low prices draw them away, and income is distributed according to ownership of factors, so those with more capital or skills earn more. This leads to efficiency but may produce inequality, so governments use taxes and transfers. In a command economy a central planning authority decides production targets and prices; distribution is more equal but shortages, queues and low innovation may arise. In a mixed economy the market allocates most private goods while the state provides public goods (roads, defence), controls harmful goods, regulates monopolies and redistributes income by progressive taxes, subsidies and social services. Indicators used to compare outcomes include the Gini coefficient, poverty rate, output growth and access to services.
sla_notes_illustrations: When cashew prices rise in a market economy, more farmers plant cashew, whereas under central planning the state would issue quotas of hectares for cashew regardless of price.
sla_notes_daily_life: The choice of system affects whether people can freely start businesses, how land is used, how prices are set for maize and fuel and how much support the poor receive.
sla_exercise: How does the price mechanism allocate resources?::Prices signal scarcity and profit so resources move to the most profitable uses.||State one weakness of resource allocation in a command economy.::Central planners may make errors causing shortages or surpluses and there is little incentive to innovate.||How does a mixed economy reduce income inequality?::Through progressive taxes, subsidies and social services.||Name one indicator of income inequality.::The Gini coefficient.

sla_notes_intro: Price theory shows how price changes affect buying decisions and firms' revenue and profit. This activity applies demand, supply and elasticity to real cases.
sla_notes_details: When price rises, the income effect and substitution effect make consumers buy less. The effect on total revenue depends on elasticity: if demand is elastic (PED greater than 1) a price rise reduces total revenue and a price fall raises it; if demand is inelastic (PED less than 1) a price rise increases revenue. Firms with inelastic products such as salt or fuel can raise prices with a small fall in sales, while sellers of luxury goods or goods with many substitutes must be careful. Pricing strategies include discounts, price discrimination and promotional prices. Consumers also respond to changes in income (normal and inferior goods) and to prices of substitutes and complements. Government price controls such as a minimum or maximum price also affect behaviour and profit.
sla_notes_illustrations: A shop sells 200 bottles at 1 000 shillings, earning 200 000. If it raises the price to 1 100 and sales fall to 190, revenue is 209 000, so demand was inelastic and the price increase raised profit, assuming costs did not rise.
sla_notes_daily_life: Retailers use sales and discounts, airlines charge different fares by season, and consumers change to cheaper brands or products when prices rise.
sla_exercise: If demand is elastic, what happens to total revenue when price rises?::Total revenue falls.||A shop sells 200 units at 1 000 shillings, then 190 units at 1 100. Compute the new revenue.::190 x 1 100 = 209 000 shillings.||Name two effects that explain why consumers buy less when the price rises.::The substitution effect and the income effect.||Give an example of a good with inelastic demand.::Salt, fuel, or basic medicine.

sla_notes_intro: Firms use cost, revenue and market information to choose the price and quantity that give the best outcome. This activity applies production, cost and market theories in decision making.
sla_notes_details: A firm compares marginal revenue (MR) and marginal cost (MC) for each extra unit: it should expand while MR is greater than MC and stop where MR = MC. A price-taking firm in perfect competition has MR equal to price, so it produces where P = MC and earns normal profit in the long run. A monopolist faces a downward-sloping demand curve, so MR is below price; it chooses the output where MR = MC and charges the price on the demand curve at that quantity, earning supernormal profit. Firms should shut down in the short run if price is below average variable cost. In an oligopoly firms consider rivals' reactions, so prices tend to be stable. Break-even analysis finds output where TR = TC, and firms use cost data to decide between produce, expand or exit.
sla_notes_illustrations: A monopolist has demand P = 50 - Q and cost C = 10Q. Then TR = 50Q - Q^2, MR = 50 - 2Q, MC = 10, so 50 - 2Q = 10 and Q = 20, P = 30 and profit = 30 x 20 - 200 = 400.
sla_notes_daily_life: Firms deciding whether to hire another worker, add a bus route or open a second shop use these ideas, as do government regulators setting utility prices.
sla_exercise: At what output does a monopolist maximise profit?::Where MR = MC.||Given P = 50 - Q and MC = 10, find the monopolist's output.::MR = 50 - 2Q = 10 so Q = 20 and P = 30.||When should a firm shut down in the short run?::When price is below average variable cost.||Why is MR equal to price in perfect competition?::Because a firm is a price taker and can sell any quantity at the market price.

sla_notes_intro: A research project trains students to investigate an economic problem using data. In Form Five they select a problem, design the study and start collecting data.
sla_notes_details: Research steps include identifying a problem (for example the effect of the price of fuel on transport fares in our ward), writing the title, background, statement of the problem, objectives and research questions, reviewing literature, choosing the method and preparing a mini-proposal. Data sources are primary (questionnaires, interviews, observation) and secondary (National Bureau of Statistics, Bank of Tanzania reports, newspapers). Sampling, such as random or purposive sampling, is used to select respondents, and ethical rules like consent and confidentiality must be followed. Data are then collected, recorded systematically and stored for analysis in Form Six. Economic variables should be clearly measurable, for example price, income, quantity and employment.
sla_notes_illustrations: A group studies the effect of price changes on the sales of vegetables in a local market, prepares a questionnaire for 20 sellers, records daily prices and quantities for two weeks and stores the data in a table.
sla_notes_daily_life: Research skills help in planning a business, understanding local economic problems and preparing for university study and policy work.

sla_notes_intro: Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole. It looks at total output, employment, the price level, money and trade rather than individual markets.
sla_notes_details: Macroeconomics is the branch of economics that deals with aggregates such as national income, total employment, the general price level, the money supply, government finance and the balance of payments. Its scope includes economic growth and development, business cycles, unemployment, inflation, money and banking, public finance and international trade. The main goals are full employment, price stability, economic growth, a favourable balance of payments, equitable distribution of income and a sustainable environment. Policies used to achieve them are fiscal policy (taxation and spending), monetary policy (money supply and interest rates) and trade and exchange rate policies. Circular flow of income shows that households supply factors to firms and receive income, spend on goods and services, and that leakages (savings, taxes, imports) are matched by injections (investment, government spending, exports).
sla_notes_illustrations: The circular flow shows that when households save more, spending falls and firms sell less, unless banks lend the savings to firms for investment, which restores the flow.
sla_notes_daily_life: Macroeconomic news such as GDP growth, inflation and interest rates affects job opportunities, loan costs, food prices and government services.
sla_exercise: Define macroeconomics.::The study of the economy as a whole, dealing with aggregates such as national income, employment and prices.||State three macroeconomic goals.::Full employment, price stability and economic growth (also balance of payments equilibrium).||Name two leakages from the circular flow.::Savings, taxes or imports.||Name two macroeconomic policy tools.::Fiscal policy and monetary policy.

sla_notes_intro: National income is the total value of goods and services produced by a country in a period, usually a year. This activity covers key terms, measuring approaches, determinants and equilibrium.
sla_notes_details: Key terms are Gross Domestic Product (GDP), the value of final output produced within a country; Gross National Product (GNP) = GDP + net income from abroad; Net National Product = GNP - depreciation; nominal GDP (current prices) and real GDP (constant prices). There are three approaches: the output approach (sum of value added by all sectors), the income approach (wages + rent + interest + profit) and the expenditure approach: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M). Real GDP = nominal GDP / GDP deflator x 100. Determinants include natural resources, labour force, capital, technology, political stability and government policy. National income raises the standard of living by increasing goods available, but per capita figures, distribution and environmental effects must also be considered. In the simple Keynesian model equilibrium occurs where Y = C + I (or where leakages equal injections), and the multiplier k = 1/(1 - MPC) shows the effect of a change in spending on income.
sla_notes_daily_life: National income statistics guide governments in planning budgets and help compare Tanzania with other countries; a rise in real GDP per person usually means better living standards.
sla_exercise: State the expenditure formula for GDP.::GDP = C + I + G + (X - M).||Find real GDP if nominal GDP is 1 200 and the deflator is 120.::Real GDP = 1 200/120 x 100 = 1 000.||If MPC = 0.8, find the multiplier.::k = 1/(1 - 0.8) = 5.||Find equilibrium income if C = 100 + 0.8Y and I = 200.::Y = 1 500.

sla_notes_intro: Unemployment exists when people who are able and willing to work at the current wage cannot find jobs. It is a major macroeconomic problem.
sla_notes_details: The labour force consists of people aged 15 and above who are employed or actively looking for work, and the unemployment rate = unemployed / labour force x 100. Forms include frictional (people between jobs or new job seekers), structural (mismatch of skills after changes in industry), cyclical (fall in aggregate demand during recession), seasonal (agriculture or tourism off-season), disguised (more workers than needed, common in family farms) and technological unemployment (machines replacing labour). Causes include rapid population growth, low investment, poor education and skills, rural-urban migration, recessions and rigid wages. Effects include loss of output and income, poverty, crime, brain drain, government spending on support and social unrest. Control measures include investment promotion, vocational and entrepreneurship training, support for small businesses and agriculture, labour market information, public works and monetary and fiscal stimulus.
sla_notes_illustrations: If the labour force is 20 million and 3 million people are without jobs, the unemployment rate is 3/20 x 100 = 15 percent.
sla_notes_daily_life: Graduates who cannot find jobs, casual labourers who work only in the harvest season and youth in urban areas illustrate unemployment in daily life.
sla_exercise: Calculate the unemployment rate if the labour force is 20 million and 3 million are unemployed.::15 percent.||What is structural unemployment?::Unemployment caused by a mismatch between workers' skills and available jobs after structural changes in the economy.||Give two effects of unemployment.::Loss of output and income, and rise in poverty and crime.||Suggest two measures to control unemployment.::Vocational and entrepreneurship training and promotion of investment in small businesses and agriculture.

sla_notes_intro: Money is anything generally accepted as a medium of exchange. This activity looks at how money developed, what it does and how central banks control it.
sla_notes_details: Before money, people used barter, exchanging goods directly, which required a double coincidence of wants. Money evolved through commodity money (cattle, salt, beads, shells), metallic money (gold, silver, copper), paper money and bank deposits, then plastic cards and electronic or mobile money such as M-Pesa. The functions of money are a medium of exchange, a unit of account, a store of value and a standard of deferred payment. Qualities include acceptability, durability, portability, divisibility, scarcity and stability of value. Monetary policy is the actions of the central bank, the Bank of Tanzania, to control the money supply and interest rates. Tools include the discount rate (Central Bank Rate), the statutory minimum reserve requirement, open market operations (buying and selling government securities), moral suasion and credit ceilings. Money multiplier = 1/reserve ratio. Contractionary policy reduces inflation, and expansionary policy raises spending and output.
sla_notes_illustrations: With a reserve requirement of 10 percent, a deposit of 1 000 000 shillings can support a maximum expansion of deposits of 1 000 000 x 1/0.1 = 10 000 000 shillings.
sla_notes_daily_life: Mobile money transfers, bank loans, savings and changes in interest rates all show money and monetary policy in daily life.
sla_exercise: Name the four functions of money.::Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value and standard of deferred payment.||What is the main problem of barter?::The need for a double coincidence of wants.||Name two tools of monetary policy.::Central bank rate and reserve requirements (or open market operations).||Find the money multiplier if the reserve ratio is 10%.::1/0.10 = 10.

learning_activity_name: Describe inflation (meaning, types, causes, effects and control measures)
sla_name: Inflation: meaning, types, causes, effects and control
sla_assessment_criteria: Inflation is well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Local economic news outlets (newspapers|Magazines|Online news platforms)|National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) reports|Bank of Tanzania (BOT) publications
sla_references: TET(2023), ECONOMICS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level over time. It reduces the purchasing power of money.
sla_notes_details: The rate of inflation = (CPI in the current year - CPI in the previous year)/CPI in the previous year x 100, where the Consumer Price Index measures the cost of a basket of goods. Types include creeping (mild), galloping, hyperinflation, demand-pull, cost-push and imported inflation, and the opposite of inflation is deflation. Causes: demand-pull inflation from excess aggregate demand or too much money; cost-push from higher wages, fuel and raw material costs; imported inflation from higher import prices; also supply shortages, exchange rate depreciation and government deficit financing. Effects: falling purchasing power, redistribution against fixed-income earners, discourages saving, raises the cost of production, reduces export competitiveness and creates uncertainty, though mild inflation may encourage investment. Control measures include monetary policy (raising interest rates), fiscal policy (reducing spending or raising taxes), increasing supply, price controls and exchange rate stability.
sla_notes_illustrations: If the CPI rises from 120 to 126 in one year then the inflation rate = (126 - 120)/120 x 100 = 5 percent.
sla_notes_daily_life: Consumers experience inflation when maize flour, transport fares and school fees cost more than the previous year while incomes remain the same.
sla_exercise: Define inflation.::A sustained rise in the general price level.||Calculate the inflation rate if CPI rises from 120 to 126.::5 percent.||Differentiate demand-pull from cost-push inflation.::Demand-pull is caused by excess total demand while cost-push is caused by rising costs of production.||Give two measures to control inflation.::Raising interest rates or reducing the money supply, and reducing government spending or raising taxes.

sla_assessment_criteria: Public finance is well described.
sla_teaching_aids: International Monetary Fund (IMF) reports|World Bank reports|TRA reports|Tax guidelines|Tax policies|Ministry of Finance reports|Budget statements|Policy documents on public finance

sla_notes_intro: Public finance studies how the government raises and spends money. It includes taxes, public borrowing and the budget.
sla_notes_details: Government revenue comes from tax sources (direct taxes such as income tax and corporate tax, and indirect taxes such as VAT and excise duty) and non-tax sources (fees, fines, licences, dividends from public enterprises), plus grants and borrowing. Taxes can be progressive (higher rate for higher incomes), proportional or regressive. Government expenditure is recurrent (salaries, operations) and development (roads, schools, energy). Budget balance = revenue - expenditure: a deficit occurs when spending exceeds revenue and it is financed by borrowing. Public debt is the total amount the government owes, both domestic (from banks and bonds) and external (from other governments and institutions such as the IMF and World Bank); debt should be used for productive investment and kept sustainable. Fiscal policy is the use of taxation and government expenditure to influence the economy: expansionary policy (cut taxes or raise spending) raises demand and jobs, while contractionary policy reduces inflation.
sla_notes_illustrations: If expected revenue is 17 trillion shillings and planned expenditure is 20 trillion, the budget deficit is 20 - 17 = 3 trillion shillings and must be financed by borrowing or grants.
sla_notes_daily_life: People see public finance when they pay VAT, PAYE or road licence fees and when the government builds schools, health centres and roads.
sla_exercise: Give two examples of indirect taxes.::Value added tax and excise duty.||Calculate the deficit if revenue is 17 trillion and expenditure is 20 trillion.::3 trillion shillings.||Differentiate a progressive from a regressive tax.::A progressive tax takes a higher percentage from higher incomes, while a regressive tax takes a higher percentage from low incomes.||What is expansionary fiscal policy?::Increasing government spending or reducing taxes to raise aggregate demand and employment.

sla_assessment_criteria: International trade well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Tanzania trade policies|Trade regulations|Tanzania Trade Development Authority (TanTrade) reports|UNCTAD reports|UNCTAD publications
sla_references: TET(2023), ECONOMICS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: International trade is the exchange of goods and services between countries. It allows specialisation and gains from trade, but may also bring problems.
sla_notes_details: Countries trade because resources, climate and technology differ. Absolute advantage exists when a country can produce a good using fewer resources than another, while comparative advantage means it has the lower opportunity cost. Under the theory of comparative advantage both countries gain if each specialises in what it produces at lower opportunity cost and trades. Advantages of trade include larger markets, efficiency, access to goods and technology, competition and lower prices; disadvantages include over-dependence, dumping, harm to infant industries, unemployment in import-competing sectors and depletion of resources. Terms of trade = (index of export prices/index of import prices) x 100. The balance of payments records all transactions with the rest of the world: the current account (goods, services, income and transfers) and the capital and financial account. Protectionism uses tariffs, quotas, subsidies and embargoes to protect local industries.
sla_notes_illustrations: Country A produces 10 maize or 5 cloth per unit of labour and B produces 6 maize or 4 cloth. Opportunity cost of one cloth is 2 maize in A and 1.5 maize in B, so B has the comparative advantage in cloth and A in maize.
sla_notes_daily_life: Importing fuel and vehicles, exporting coffee and minerals, and tariffs on imported goods show international trade in daily life.
sla_exercise: Differentiate absolute from comparative advantage.::Absolute advantage means producing with fewer resources, comparative advantage means producing at a lower opportunity cost.||If export price index is 110 and import price index is 125, find the terms of trade.::110/125 x 100 = 88.||Name two tools of protectionism.::Tariffs and quotas.||What are the two main parts of the balance of payments?::The current account and the capital and financial account.

sla_notes_intro: Macroeconomic theories help explain the health of an economy using data on growth, prices, employment and trade. Students collect and interpret such data.
sla_notes_details: To describe the state of an economy, collect data on real GDP growth, inflation, unemployment, interest rates, exchange rate, public debt, the balance of payments and the current account for several years, and present them in tables and graphs. Use classical theory (flexible prices and self-adjusting markets), Keynesian theory (demand-led output and the multiplier) and monetarist theory (money supply and inflation) to interpret. A growth rate is (GDP this year - GDP last year)/GDP last year x 100. A rising GDP with low inflation and low unemployment shows a healthy economy, while high inflation with low growth suggests overheating or supply problems and a widening trade deficit shows weak export competitiveness. For international comparisons use per capita income, terms of trade and trade openness (X + M)/GDP. Findings are presented in a report with conclusions and policy recommendations.
sla_notes_illustrations: If real GDP grows from 100 to 106 billion the growth rate is 6 percent; with inflation at 4 percent and unemployment falling, the economy is judged to be expanding steadily.
sla_notes_daily_life: News about a rising exchange rate, slower growth or a new budget can be understood and explained using these data and theories.
sla_exercise: Name three indicators used to describe the state of an economy.::Real GDP growth, inflation and unemployment (also exchange rate or trade balance).||Compute the growth rate when GDP rises from 100 to 106.::6 percent.||Which theory stresses the role of money supply in inflation?::Monetarist theory.||What is trade openness?::The sum of exports and imports as a share of GDP.

sla_teaching_aids: Journals of Development Economics|Journals of Economic Growth|World Bank reports|International Monetary Fund (IMF) reports

sla_notes_intro: Countries differ in their levels of development. Macroeconomic theories and indicators explain why some nations are more developed than others.
sla_notes_details: Economic growth is an increase in real output, while economic development includes improvements in living standards, health, education and equality. Indicators include GDP per capita, the Human Development Index (life expectancy, years of schooling and income), poverty rate, literacy, infant mortality and the Gini coefficient. Developed countries have high income, industrialised economies and strong institutions, whereas developing countries have low incomes, reliance on agriculture and primary exports, high population growth and limited infrastructure. Theories include Rostow's stages of growth, the Harrod-Domar model (growth depends on savings and the capital-output ratio: g = s/v), dependency theory and endogenous growth theory (human capital and technology). Causes of underdevelopment include low savings and investment, weak institutions, poor infrastructure, debt burden, unfavourable terms of trade and conflict. Policies include investment in education and health, industrialisation, good governance and regional integration.
sla_notes_illustrations: In the Harrod-Domar model, if the savings rate is 20 percent and the capital-output ratio is 4, the growth rate is 20/4 = 5 percent; raising savings to 24 percent gives 6 percent growth.
sla_notes_daily_life: Access to clean water, schools, hospitals and electricity in a region are direct signs of the level of development experienced by citizens.
sla_exercise: Differentiate economic growth from economic development.::Growth is an increase in real output, while development also includes better health, education, equality and living standards.||Name the three components of the Human Development Index.::Life expectancy (health), education (years of schooling) and income per capita.||In the Harrod-Domar model find g when s = 20% and v = 4.::g = 20/4 = 5 percent.||Give two characteristics of developing countries.::Low per capita income and dependence on agriculture and primary exports.

sla_assessment_criteria: Simple software to analyse data collected in Form Five is well used.
sla_teaching_aids: Academic journals|Research project guidelines|Sample of research projects
sla_references: TET(2023), ECONOMICS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: In Form Six students analyse the data collected in Form Five and write and submit the project report.
sla_notes_details: Students first organise data in tables and code them, then use simple software such as spreadsheets to compute totals, averages, percentages and growth rates and to draw charts. Findings are interpreted using economic theory, for example demand and supply or elasticity, and linked to the research questions. The report has a title page, abstract, acknowledgements, table of contents, introduction, objectives, literature review, methodology, findings and discussion, conclusion, recommendations, references and appendices. References are listed using a consistent style, and the report is written in clear language with correct citations. The report is submitted on time and presented to the teacher and classmates, who ask questions and give feedback.
sla_notes_illustrations: A group that studied vegetable prices uses a spreadsheet to compute the average price for each week, draws a line graph, finds that prices fell 15 percent in the harvest week and explains this using increased supply.
sla_notes_daily_life: Analysing data with software and writing reports are skills that are useful in banks, government offices, businesses and further study.
sla_exercise: Name two things a spreadsheet can do in data analysis.::Compute totals, averages and percentages and draw charts.||List four sections of a project report.::Introduction, methodology, findings and conclusion (also abstract and references).||Why are recommendations included in the report?::To suggest actions that solve the economic problem studied.||How would you show a price change of 20 to 17 as a percentage?::(17 - 20)/20 x 100 = -15 percent, a fall of 15 percent.
